description: We’re a team of friends from Dushanbe, Tajikistan: developers and AI/data enthusiasts working on Field Shift. Our goal is a tool that helps Central Asian farmers plan crop rotations with NASA data to save water and restore soil. We have experience building AI products and placing at hackathons. We’re looking for people strong in data analysis/GIS, frontend development, and design or pitching.
summary: Dehqon AI ("dehqon" means "farmer" in Tajik) is a web decision-support tool that helps smallholder farmers in Tajikistan choose a 4-year crop rotation. A farmer marks the field on a satellite map, picks the crops of the last three years, and sets priorities (save water, healthy soil, low risk, income) and how much irrigation water is available. Dehqon AI reads 10 years of NASA POWER daily climate and NASA MODIS NDVI for that field plus ISRIC SoilGrids soil data, simulates all 14,641 rotations year by year (water balance, heat stress, salinity, soil carbon and nitrogen), removes those that break agronomic rules, and shows three different Pareto-optimal plans next to "carry on as now". For a demo field near Bokhtar, the best plan needs 19% less irrigation water over 4 years, raises the soil health index from 52 to 70 (instead of 52 to 48) and cuts the modeled harvest loss in a dry, hot year from 50% to 22%. Every number shows its data source and confidence. Answers come in plain words for farmers or with full numbers for agronomists, in Tajik, Russian and English.
details: WHAT IT DOES Dehqon AI turns NASA Earth observations into a concrete answer for one field: what to sow this year and in the next three years. The farmer marks the field (a point with its area, or the field outline) on a satellite map, chooses the crops of the last three years from 26 crops, sets four priorities from 0 to 5 (save water, healthy soil, low risk, income) and says how much irrigation water the farm gets (enough, limited, rain only). The result is three different 4-year plans, each compared with continuing as now: irrigation water in m3 per hectare, soil health, and the share of the harvest lost in a dry, hot year. A season calendar, a 3D view of the field, a "build your own rotation" check, six "what if the year is different" scenarios and 10 years of NASA data for the field complete the picture. HOW IT WORKS 1. Field profile: 10 years of daily NASA POWER climate (rain, temperature, humidity, solar radiation, soil wetness), MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI (250 m) and ISRIC SoilGrids soil (organic carbon, pH, texture, 0-30 cm). 2. Simulation: for each crop and year the model computes crop water need from reference evapotranspiration (Hargreaves-Samani, FAO-56), effective rainfall (FAO/AGLW), irrigation limited by the water available, yield response to water deficit (FAO-33, Ky), heat stress (days above 35 C), salinity, repeat-crop losses and nitrogen from legumes, and updates soil carbon, nitrogen, salinity and structure. 3. Search: the 11 crops that suit the field best enter a full search of 11^4 = 14,641 rotations. Rotations that break agronomic rules (crop repeats, return intervals, family limits) are removed, the rest are scored on water, soil, risk and income, and three different Pareto-optimal plans are shown using the farmer's priorities. 4. Honest data: every source shows its type (reanalysis, satellite, model), resolution, download date and confidence. If live data is not available for a field, the tool waits and retries instead of borrowing data from another place. 5. Two ways to read the answer: plain words for farmers, or a specialist table with units and methods for agronomists. An assistant chat answers questions about the field and the plans. WHY IT MATTERS In Khatlon, NASA POWER shows about 89 days a year hotter than 35 C (2016-2025, near Bokhtar), and rain covers only about a quarter of the water the fields lose to evaporation. Repeating cotton and wheat depletes and salinizes the soil. For the demo field near Bokhtar, the best plan uses 19% less irrigation water over 4 years, raises the soil health index from 52 to 70 instead of falling to 48, and lowers the modeled loss in a dry, hot year from 50% to 22%. These are model estimates; our next step is a pilot with 5-10 farms near Bokhtar and Vakhsh together with an agronomist. TOOLS Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS and Three.js (frontend on Vercel); a TypeScript API on Supabase Edge Functions with a Postgres cache; a Python (FastAPI, pytest) reference model kept in parity with the TypeScript model. Interface in Tajik, Russian and English. USE OF AI TOOLS We used AI coding assistants (Anthropic Claude) to help write code, texts and documentation. The in-app assistant chat uses the DeepSeek API; it only explains, while all numbers come from our transparent model. The demo video voiceover is synthesized speech (macOS text-to-speech), and the video description says so. No NASA logos or branding were generated.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources), daily agroclimatology API
NASA MODIS MOD13Q1 v061 NDVI (250 m, 16-day), via the ORNL DAAC MODIS web service
NASA GIBS: MODIS Terra Corrected Reflectance (true color) daily imagery
projectRefs: ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0 (soil organic carbon, pH, texture, 250 m)
FAO-56 Crop evapotranspiration (method for crop water needs)
FAO-66 Crop yield response to water
AWS Terrain Tiles (elevation for the 3D views)
Next.js and React (web app, hosted on Vercel)
Supabase (Edge Functions API and Postgres cache)
Anthropic Claude (AI coding and writing assistant, SI)
